s1.syndrome_frame: chronic, painful, growing tumor on the buttock with secondary infection and possible viral etiology
salient_findings: growing, painful tumor on the right buttock
verrucous, exophytic tumor with yellow drainage
positive for HSV type 2 and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
key_facts: 8-month history of a growing tumor
tumor located on the right medial buttock
tumor extends to the perianal skin
patient has chronic kidney disease
patient has genital herpes simplex virus (HSV)
no history of genital warts, HIV, or inflammatory bowel disease
physical examination findings revealed a 5 × 7-cm tumor
superficial bacterial cultures grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
microbial cultures were negative for deep fungal infection and acid-fast bacteria
biopsy showed hyperplastic epidermis with ulceration, necrosis, and dense inflammatory infiltrate
immunohistochemistry showed positive staining for herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2

per_call: Eczema herpeticum with secondary bacterial infection

shortlist.label: Verrucous carcinoma
shortlist.why_kept: The patient's 8-month history of a growing, painful tumor on the buttock with a verrucous appearance is consistent with this diagnosis

shortlist.label: Buschke-Lowenstein tumor
shortlist.why_kept: The tumor's location on the buttock, its size, and the presence of HSV infection are consistent with this rare but aggressive form of squamous cell carcinoma

shortlist.label: Giant condyloma acuminatum
shortlist.why_kept: The tumor's appearance and location, as well as the patient's history of genital HSV, are consistent with this diagnosis

shortlist.label: Squamous cell carcinoma
shortlist.why_kept: The patient's tumor has features consistent with squamous cell carcinoma, including hyperplastic epidermis and dense inflammatory infiltrate

shortlist.label: Herpes simplex virus infection
shortlist.why_kept: The presence of HSV type 2 in the tumor, as confirmed by immunohistochemistry, suggests that HSV infection is contributing to the patient's condition

raw.rationale: The patient's presentation of a large, verrucous, exophytic tumor with positive staining for herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2, along with a history of genital HSV, is most consistent with Buschke-Lowenstein tumor, a rare and aggressive form of condyloma acuminatum associated with HPV and often secondary to HSV infection.

rejected.label: Verrucous carcinoma
rejected.why: While verrucous carcinoma can present similarly, the presence of HSV and the specific histological features point more towards Buschke-Lowenstein tumor.

rejected.label: Giant condyloma acuminatum
rejected.why: Giant condyloma acuminatum is another term for Buschke-Lowenstein tumor, but the specific mention of HSV infection and the aggressive nature of the tumor make Buschke-Lowenstein tumor the more precise diagnosis.

rejected.label: Squamous cell carcinoma
rejected.why: Squamous cell carcinoma does not typically present with the same level of viral association as seen in this case, and the histological features are more specific to a condylomatous lesion.

rejected.label: Herpes simplex virus infection
rejected.why: While the patient has a history of genital HSV and the tumor stains positive for HSV, the primary issue is the tumor itself, which is best described as a Buschke-Lowenstein tumor rather than simply an HSV infection.
